planting.note: Direct sow or set out young plants in spring into lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species resents rich or damp ground, which quickly leads to floppy growth and crown rot.

directions: Balkan yarrow is a compact, silvery-leaved species from the Balkan Peninsula grown in gardens chiefly as one of the two wild parents behind the popular hybrid cultivar 'Moonshine.' Site it in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since rich or damp ground quickly leads to floppy growth and crown rot. Flat-topped clusters of bright yellow flowers rise above finely dissected, woolly gray-green foliage from late spring into summer, drawing bees and other pollinators. Once established it shrugs off drought and poor soil, needing only an occasional post-bloom shearing to stay tidy and encourage rebloom.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out young plants in spring into lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, mimicking the rocky mountain slopes where this species grows wild.

directions: Taygetos yarrow is a silver-leaved species native to the rocky slopes of Greece's Taygetos mountains, best known in cultivation as the other wild parent of the popular hybrid 'Moonshine' yarrow. Grow it in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun, the same tough conditions it experiences in its native mountain habitat. Pale primrose-yellow, flat-topped flower clusters open above finely cut, aromatic gray foliage from early summer onward, attracting bees and butterflies. It is highly drought-tolerant once established and, like other mountain yarrows, resents heavy, poorly drained soil and high humidity.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring into average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; this Coastal Plain native is less cold-hardy than most bluestars and does best where winters are mild.

directions: Stiff bluestar is a Coastal Plain native found in wet pinewoods and swamp margins from Georgia and Florida west to Mississippi, where it forms upright, unbranched clumps of narrow, willow-like leaves. It served as one of the two wild parents of the compact hybrid 'Starstruck', contributing its neat, non-flopping habit to that shorter garden selection. Clusters of pale blue, star-shaped flowers open in late spring atop the clump, followed by rich butter-yellow fall foliage color. Established clumps are drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and essentially maintenance-free once sited in average to moist, well-drained soil.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring into lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; spike lavender tolerates heat and drought better than English lavender but is noticeably less cold-hardy.

directions: Spike lavender is a heat-loving Mediterranean species native to lower, warmer elevations than English lavender, and it is one of the two parents that give rise to sterile lavandin hybrids such as 'Grosso' and 'Provence.' Its broader, gray-green leaves and camphor-rich scent set it apart from the sweeter, narrower-leaved English lavender, and its oil is prized more for industrial and cleaning-product fragrances than for fine perfumery. Plant in lean, sharply drained, alkaline soil in full sun; it tolerates heat and drought better than English lavender but is noticeably less cold-hardy. Shear back after the summer flush of pale lavender-blue flower spikes to keep the rounded shrub from sprawling and to encourage denser regrowth.
sources: Purdue University New Crops Resource Online Program

common_name: Luther Hill Sweet Corn (Historic White Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow 1 inch deep in blocks of at least 4 rows after last frost for reliable wind pollination; Luther Hill is a compact, heavily suckering plant that benefits from wide spacing to let side shoots also produce ears.

directions: Luther Hill was bred by New Jersey farmer Luther Hill in 1902 and became the most popular sweet corn in parts of New Jersey for half a century before serving as a direct parent of the later hybrid 'Silver Queen'. Plants stay relatively compact at around five and a half feet, typically producing two small, tender white-kerneled ears per stalk plus extra ears on the vigorous suckers if given room to spread. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the danger of frost has passed, planting in blocks for dependable pollination. The flavor is notably sweet and rich even by modern standards, which is why breeders have continued to draw on its genetics long after more productive hybrids replaced it commercially.
sources: Fedco Seeds — Luther Hill Organic White Sweet Corn

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer for a fall and winter harvest, or in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; a hard frost sweetens the flavor considerably.

directions: Siberian kale is an old, extremely cold-hardy strain of Brassica napus grown across northern Russia and Siberia long before it reached North American seed catalogs, and it stands behind many of the popular 'Russian' type kales, including the purple-stemmed Red Russian selections bred from it. Unlike the tightly curled Scots kales of Brassica oleracea, Siberian kale has flat, deeply lobed, blue-green leaves with a milder, sweeter flavor that improves further after frost. Direct sow into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings to about a foot apart, and harvest outer leaves continually as the plant regrows from the center. It tolerates hard freezes better than almost any other garden brassica, often surviving under snow cover well into winter.
sources: Seed Ambassadors Project — Russian & Siberian Kale
North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Brassica napus Pabularia Group

planting.note: Direct sow in cool weather into average, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike baby-leaf cress types, Persian cress is usually left to grow tall for its airy sprays of seed pods rather than cut young.

directions: Persian cress is a distinct, upright-growing strain of garden cress grown less for cutting as salad microgreens and more for its tall, airy sprays of tiny silvery seed pods, prized by floral designers as a delicate cut-flower filler. Left to mature past the baby-leaf stage, plants send up branched, wiry stems topped with small white flowers that quickly form the decorative seed heads for which the variety is grown. Direct sow in cool weather into average, well-drained soil in full sun, thinning seedlings a few inches apart to give the branching stems room to develop. Succession sow every few weeks in spring and fall for a continuous supply of cutting stems, since plants bolt and decline quickly once summer heat arrives.

planting.note: Direct sow thickly and shallowly as soon as the soil can be worked, keeping the seedbed evenly moist since the mucilage-coated seed needs constant moisture to germinate evenly.

directions: Curly cress is the finely ruffled, deeply frilled-leaf type of garden cress most familiar from grocery-store cress punnets, its tight curled leaf margins distinguishing it from smooth-leaved garden cress and giving each cutting a decorative, parsley-like texture. It grows fast enough to be cut as tender baby greens within a few weeks of sowing, or left a little longer for a fuller, more mustard-forward peppery bite. Direct sow thickly and shallowly into moist, cool soil, since the mucilage-coated seed needs to stay damp to germinate evenly. Succession sow every two weeks through the cool season and provide light afternoon shade in warm weather to slow bolting and keep the ruffled leaves tender.
sources: True Leaf Market — Curled Cress Seeds
Annie's Heirloom Seeds — Organic Curled Cress
